newsitem.title: USA: U.S. cancer panel tackles mammogram controversy.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cancer panel tackles mammogram controversy.

text.p: National Cancer Institute advisers Tuesday shied away from giving any specific timetable for when women should start having breast cancer screening tests, or mammograms.

Citing uncertainty in the data, the panel for now avoided recommending an age, instead promoting the idea of trying to give women the information they need to evaluate their risk of breast cancer and to make their own choices about screening.

Experts agree that mammograms save lives in women aged 50-69 and that they are not routinely needed during the 20s and 30s. But doubts about mammograms for women in the "transitional" decade of the 40s have caused controversy.

The most recent studies suggest that mammograms in that age group can cut breast cancer deaths by about 17 percent, although the benefits may not show up until a women is older. But the conclusions are not as clear cut as experts would like, partly because much of the data available involve women who are closer to 50 than to 40.

"You can hang your hat on (the 17 percent estimate) but you better realise it's a big hat," said Donald Berry, a Duke University statistician who summarized the results of eight international studies to the NCI advisory board.
"We cannot create certainty where it does not exist," NCI director Dr. Richard Klausner said.

Barbara Rimer, a Duke Medical Centre cancer expert who heads the panel, said there was no "magic" age to solve the debate neatly. "It's not going to be as simple as you'd like it to be," she told reporters after the meeting.

A separate panel of independent scientific advisers, forming what is known as a consensus conference, last month reviewed scientific data on mammograms for women in their 40s. Their draft report, which is still being refined, ignited more controversy by saying women should make up their own minds.
The NCI's advisory panel Tuesday did not reach any final conclusions, instead setting up a subcommittee to press on with the task over the next few months.
The group ultimately may decide to be more specific but the emphasis Tuesday was less on telling women what to do than on helping them weigh their own risks.

Mammograms are currently the best tool for breast cancer detection, but they miss many cancers, particularly in women in their 40s who have denser breast tissue. And four out of five of the suspicious lesions they do detect in this age group turn out to be benign after further testing or biopsies.
